nodes.label: Carl Berger
nodes.date_label: The Sense of Power 1970 · The Writing of Canadian History 1976; 2nd ed. 1986
nodes.description: A University of Toronto historian of English-Canadian ideas. The Sense of Power (1970) is 'a study in Canadian nationalist thought': against the 'so-called liberal nationalist school', for which imperialism and nationalism added up to 'a struggle between the past and the future', he argued that 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission'. The Writing of Canadian History (1976; second edition 1986) examines 'aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century' through the 'central teachings' of Wrong, Shortt, Martin, Innis, Lower, Underhill, Creighton and Morton, and treats written history as 'a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'; he left French-Canadian writing aside because the two language traditions had been 'preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”'. In period, Jacques Monet thought the imperialism thesis 'très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (1972), while Douglas Cole and Graham Carr held that it over-Canadianized a Britannic movement, Susan Mann Trofimenkoff called his imperialists' nationalism 'decidedly masculine' (1979), Allen Mills found that his account of all Canadian historians as nationalists put 'much too much weight on that over-used term' (1977), and Ronald Rudin rejected his assumption that historians were 'united by their search for the truth' (1997).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carl Berger (b. 1939); ed., Imperialism and Nationalism, 1884–1914: A Conflict in Canadian Thought (1969); The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (1970; 2nd ed. 2013, with an introduction by Doug Owram); The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970 (1976; 2nd ed., … since 1900, 1986, with a new chapter, 'Tradition and the “New” History'); Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983). Readings: Monet (1972); Mills (1977); Terry Cook (1977–78); Trofimenkoff (1979); Carr (1982); Karr (1989); Rudin (1997). Later reading: Owram (2013).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the two framework books. Neither could be read continuously: both are borrow-only on the Internet Archive. Berger's own words are quoted from Google Books snippet views (The Sense of Power, 2013 printing with the 1970 pagination: introduction pp. 3, 9–10, conclusion p. 259; The Writing of Canadian History, 1986 edition: both prefaces and pp. 181, 261–262, 289, 298, 312), and are corroborated by in-period reviews read in full: Monet (1972), Mills (1977) and Terry Cook (1977–78). Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983) is checked at metadata level only. He is not presented as the originator of the imperialism thesis: Monet notes that Norman Penlington's Canada and Imperialism (1965) had already suggested it. Contested in period: Page, Cole and Nelles (1970, as Monet reports them), Cole (1971), Carr (1982, journal abstract), Karr (1989) on the elite group-biography method, Trofimenkoff (1979) on women, and Rudin (1997) on French-Canadian writing and on the assumption of a common search for truth. No in-period text found here faults The Writing of Canadian History for treating only male historians; Trofimenkoff's critique is of the field. Owram's 2013 introduction is a later reading.

nodes.label: Ramsay Cook
nodes.date_label: “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” 1967 · The Maple Leaf Forever 1971 · “Regionalism Unmasked” 1983 · The Regenerators 1985 · “Cabbages Not Kings” 1990 · “Identities Are Not Like Hats” 2000
nodes.description: An English-Canadian historian of nationalism, Quebec and Victorian thought. Attacking a nationalist manifesto in the centennial year, he suggested that 'instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found' (1967, as quoted by Buckner); Careless made 'limited identities' a programme in 1969. Cook did not make region his unit of analysis: reviewing regional syntheses, he doubted 'the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions' and judged that 'as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (1983). The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social critics as replacing 'man's salvation' with 'a concern for social salvation', so that Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (as quoted by Gauvreau); Michael Gauvreau answered in 1991 that the book rests on 'military metaphors' that recent studies had abandoned, and a 1998 review named Cook, with David Marshall, the strongest advocate of the 'secularization thesis'. His lecture 'Cabbages Not Kings' (1990) proposed an ecological reading of contact in which 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world'. In the quarrel over national history he called the debate between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians' 'arid' (1993), and in 2000 he argued that identities are 'contingent' and 'multiple rather than single'.

Readings: Careless (1969); Gaffield (1986); Karr (1989); Gauvreau (1991); Marshall (1993–94); Buckner (2000).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: three of Cook's Acadiensis review essays in full (1977, 1983, 1993), the opening of the 1967 article (OpenAlex text) and the abstract of his 2000 forum piece. He is not presented as a founder: Buckner says Cook coined 'limited identities' and Careless popularized it, and Cook wrote in 1995 that the phrase was 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (quoted by Buckner). Contested in period: Gauvreau (1991) on The Regenerators and on limited identities as a frame that marginalized religion; Karr (1989) on his 'anti-national crusade'; Buckner (2000) on the additive idea of identity he attributes to Cook and Careless. Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) is read only in its abstract, which does not name Cook.

nodes.label: J. M. S. Careless
nodes.date_label: “Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History” 1954 · Brown of the Globe 1959–63 · “‘Limited Identities’ in Canada” 1969 · “Limited Identities — Ten Years Later” 1981 · Frontier and Metropolis 1989
nodes.description: A University of Toronto historian of nineteenth-century Canada and biographer of George Brown (Brown of the Globe, 1959–63). 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954) criticised the Canadian historians who had adapted Turner's frontier thesis and proposed instead the study of the metropolis, a city that organizes a wide area 'through control of communications, trade, and finance'; in that view the frontier 'is in the largest sense a dependent', though 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism'. In 1969 he took up Ramsay Cook's phrase and argued that the Canadian experience must be understood through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class' (as quoted by Buckner, 2000); a decade later he added that 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism' and that limited identities 'should not limit his own perception' (1981). Frontier and Metropolis (1989), based on his 1987 Creighton Lectures, restated both themes. In period, Donald Davis (1985) judged his metropolitan approach 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research', and Phillip Buckner (2000) rejected the view, which he attributed to Careless and Granatstein, of regionalism as 'a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'.

Readings: Davis (1985); Szostak (1990); Irwin (1997); Buckner (2000).

The 1969 article is unread here: its wording is taken from Buckner's quotations and from Careless's own quotation of its last page in 1981. Frontier and Metropolis and Brown of the Globe are unread (catalogue records; the book's content through Szostak's review). He is not presented as the originator of either idea. In 1954 he credits metropolitanism to Lower, to Masters's Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in N. S. B. Gras, and to the Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton (pp. 16–17); Davis (1985, p. 97) notes that Lower discussed metropolitanism 'some eight years before'. He wrote in 1981 that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”' but acquired it from Ramsay Cook, so that his 1969 article 'was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea'; Cook's coinage belongs to Cook's entry. Contested in period: by W. L. Morton and S. D. Clark (both as quoted by Davis), by Davis (1985), by Szostak (1990), by Irwin (1997, abstract) and by Buckner (2000). Michael Bliss (1991–92) is not recorded as a critic of Careless: Buckner (2000, p. 9) pairs Bliss's fragmentation charge with Careless's own later worry.

nodes.label: Donald Creighton
nodes.date_label: The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence 1937 · Dominion of the North 1944 · John A. Macdonald 1952, 1955 · CHA presidential address 1957 · “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” 1969 · Canada’s First Century 1970
nodes.description: A Toronto historian whose The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) built Canadian history around the one river system 'that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent', which inspired Canadians 'to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (his own restatement of 1969); Dominion of the North (1944) calls the river 'the natural basis of a great commercial empire' and beaver fur 'the first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system'. His two-volume John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955) completed what he called 'a trilogy on one theme'; in 1969 he accepted 'the parentage of an idea' others called 'the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history', but rejected the story that his first book was 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis'. As president of the Canadian Historical Association (1957) he attacked the Liberal 'Authorized Version' of Canadian history and the imported 'Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'Frontier thesis', and in 1969 he traced the 'decline and fall' of the Empire of the St. Lawrence and of the Canada built on it, calling official bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation'. Contested in period: Michel Brunet (1953) found the Macdonald biography full of 'nombreux préjugés', Guy Frégault (1955) asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ?', and W. L. Morton, as Davis (1985) reports him, held that the metropolitan view he associated with Creighton seemed 'necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland'. From the late 1960s the national frame the Laurentian narrative supported gave way to regional history and 'limited identities' (Buckner, 2000).

Readings: Heaton (1938); Brunet (1953); Frégault (1955); Woodcock (1979); Ouellet (1984); Davis (1985); Salmon (1997); Buckner (2000).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the Laurentian narrative and Creighton's later nationalism. Read on 2026-10-14: his 1957 presidential address (pp. 1–12) and his 1969 lecture 'The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence' (pp. 14–25), both in full from page images; Dominion of the North (1944) at its contents and selected pages (pp. 21, 24–25, 166, 270, 272, 298, 419, 505–507) in an open Internet Archive copy. The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) itself is unread: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only, and its argument is checked through the 1944 book, his own 1969 retrospect (labelled as such) and the first page of Herbert Heaton's 1938 review. He is not presented as the founder of a school: in 1969 he reported that others regarded the 1937 phrase as 'the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school' and the 'genesis' of 'the Laurentian interpretation', and said only that he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea'. The Innis lineage is recorded as contested: readers from Woodcock (1979) and Ouellet (1984) to Salmon (1997) tie the book to Innis's staple studies, while Creighton said the subject was suggested by W. P. M. Kennedy, 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time'. The 1957 and 1969 texts are polemics; their judgements of Mackenzie King, Quebec and bilingualism are recorded as his claims, not adopted. Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) and his later hinterland critique are known here only through Davis (1985); Careless's 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism' (1954), Berger's chapter on Creighton (1976), Canada's First Century (1970) and the Innis biography (1957) are unread (catalogue or review level only).

nodes.label: Joy Parr
nodes.date_label: Labouring Children 1980 · 'Nature and Hierarchy' 1985 · The Gender of Breadwinners 1990 · 'Gender History and Historical Practice' 1995 · Domestic Goods 1999 · Sensing Changes 2010
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of work, gender, childhood, consumption and the environment. In 1985 she wrote that what set women and children apart as historical subjects was not nature but 'proximity to power', and asked historians to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict'. The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) tested this in two Ontario towns, Paris, a knitting-mill town where most wage earners were women, and Hanover, a furniture town where most were men; reviewers quote it rejecting 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' and treating 'class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' as pairs whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. In the Left History exchange of 1995–96 Iacovetta and Kealey called her 'a major figure in the field' of gender history, while Sangster criticised the tie her 1995 essay drew between gender history and 'the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships'; the labour historian Craig Heron praised the book but found that it had 'suppressed the impact of class' in a 1949 strike. Labouring Children (1980) grew from her Yale thesis on British child immigrants; later books turned to postwar household goods (Domestic Goods, 1999) and to sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change (Sensing Changes, 2010).

nodes.scope_note: Her own words are read in 'Nature and Hierarchy' (Atlantis, 1985, pp. 39–44, in full), the first-page extract of the 1988 CSSH article and the abstract of the 1999 ILWCH article. Her books are not read here: The Gender of Breadwinners, Domestic Goods and Sensing Changes are quoted only as their reviewers quote them, with the reviewers' page references, and the 1995 CHR essay only as Iacovetta and Kealey (1996) and Sangster (1996) quote it. She is not presented as a founder: her 1985 essay places itself among 'a good many others' asking for the change, and the Canadian gender-history debate also turned on Pierson (1991) and Scott. The 1995 CHR essay appeared in an issue of historiographical essays, not in a CHR exchange; the exchange that took it up was in Left History. The environmental work dates from 2006–10 and is used only for the environment edge; a 2026 CHR forum on The Gender of Breadwinners is a later reading.

nodes.label: Mariana Valverde
nodes.date_label: “The Struggles of the Immoral” (with Weir) 1988 · The Age of Light, Soap, and Water 1991 · “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” 1992 · Diseases of the Will 1998 · Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge 2003
nodes.description: A sociologist and criminologist, not a historian by training (PhD in social and political thought, York, 1982; University of Toronto Centre of Criminology from 1993); historians read her study of social purity in English Canada as a statement of moral regulation. The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) follows reformers who sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' and argues that their movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class'; her notes trace the term to Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch but 'restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity', and she held, as 'Foucault and his followers have pointed out', that 'the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'. In 1992 she endorsed Mitchell Dean's argument that classical liberalism was 'a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation' and faulted Jean-Marie Fecteau's account of relief institutions as means of class control as 'a rather functionalist formulation'. Historians used and contested the frame: Tina Loo asked that it 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance' (1992), Donald Wright found that the reformers' silent audiences gave 'the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (1995), and Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau wrote that she and Doug Owram 'have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from “progressive” currents of modern thought and social action' (1996). Later books turn to alcohol and the will (Diseases of the Will, 1998) and to law (Law's Dream of a Common Knowledge, 2003).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Mariana Valverde (b. 1955); “The Struggles of the Immoral: Preliminary Remarks on Moral Regulation” (with Lorna Weir, Resources for Feminist Research, 1988); “Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?” (Labour/Le Travail, 1990); The Age of Light, Soap, and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991; reissued 2008 with a new introduction); “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” (Labour/Le Travail, 1992); Gender Conflicts (ed. with Franca Iacovetta, 1992); Studies in Moral Regulation (ed., 1994); “Deconstructive Marxism” (Labour/Le Travail, 1995); Diseases of the Will: Alcohol and the Dilemmas of Freedom (1998). After 2000: Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge (2003); “Introduction to the 2008 Edition” of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water. In-period readings: Loo, Dehli and McCormick (reviews, 1992); Wright (1995); Christie and Gauvreau (1996); Strange and Loo, Making Good (1997); Hunt (1997, 1999).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-14: her review essays 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians' (1990) and 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State' (1992) in full, and 'Deconstructive Marxism' (1995) at pp. 329–332; four in-period reviews or review essays of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water in full (Loo 1992, Dehli 1992, McCormick 1992) or in their Valverde section (Wright 1995, pp. 122–126). The book itself is known here only through those reviewers' quotations and through search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, which keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text (checked: pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 match the 1992 reviewers' page references; the 1991 preface's p. 9 appears as p. ix). Christie and Gauvreau (1996), Strange and Loo (1997), Hunt (1999) and Diseases of the Will (1998) are known only through such snippets. 'The Struggles of the Immoral' (1988, with Lorna Weir) is unread. She is not presented as the originator of moral regulation: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits their theorization as 'influential here' while finding that it obscures 'the agencies of regulation internal to civil society'. She called herself a sociologist working between disciplines; Loo (1992) and Wright (1995) read her that way, and the 2008 introduction, a later reading, says that 'no history department in Canada would ever hire me'. The 2003 book is cited at title level only; the 2008 introduction is a later reading and carries no claim about the 1990s.

edges.relationship: Canadian imperialism read as one form of Canadian nationalism, through the ideas of its leading spokesmen (1970)
edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The introduction opens 'This book is a study in Canadian nationalist thought' (p. 3). Of the earlier critics he writes that 'When critics belaboured imperialism because of its hostility to “Canadian nationalism” what they really meant was that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed. There have been many varieties of Canadian nationalism'; imperialism was 'one variety of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission' (p. 9). His method: 'inquiring into the ideas and ideals which men in the past read into their interpretations of Canada and by exploring the relationship between these conceptions and the environment in which they circulated' (p. 10). The conclusion opens 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism' (p. 259). In-period reception. Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, pp. 274–276, read in full): the book's 'grande originalité' is to conclude that the imperialists were not 'des agents d'une puissance étrangère' but 'de vrais Canadians nationalistes' (pp. 274–275); the thesis, 'déjà suggérée par la monographie de Norman Penlington', 'sera dorénavant très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (p. 275); the book is 'une contribution majeure — sinon un premier modèle — à l'histoire des idées (oui, il y en a) au Canada anglophone' (p. 276). Monet also reports the first criticisms (p. 275 and nn. 2–4): neglect of the economic and military sides of imperialism (Robert Page, JCS 1970), the folding into a Canadianizing ideology of witnesses 'qui seraient plutôt des représentants du pan-britannisme' (Douglas Cole, JCS 1970), and too much weight on 'une petite élite' of intellectuals (H. V. Nelles, Canadian Forum 1970); Page, Cole (1970) and Nelles are not read here. Cole's 1971 comparative article (notes read; body closed) says that Berger 'makes the strongest case for a Canadian nationalistic consciousness within these terms' (n. 33). Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979, read): he 'manages to suspend the reader's initial disbelief and argue persuasively that turn-of-the-century imperialists were really nationalists', but 'Their nationalism and their imperialism were, however, decidedly masculine affairs' (p. 10); intellectual history 'will have to take women into account' (p. 10). Clarence Karr (1989, re-read): Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' (p. 161); 'Carl Berger's critics accuse him of an over-Canadianization of imperialism and of ignoring a broader Anglo-Saxon perspective in what Graham Carr refers to as a “scavenger hunt for nationalism”' (pp. 162–163); since his book, group biography 'has been upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method of addressing the Canadian intellectual tradition' (p. 167), and its premise that imperialism can 'only be understood in relation to the characters who espoused it and who came to personify it' risks making thought 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe' (p. 168). Carr's article (JCS 1982) is checked at its journal abstract only. A contribution, not an origin: Monet credits Penlington with the suggestion. Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Doug Owram's introduction to the 2013 edition (snippet view) calls it 'pretty much the standard interpretation of the way in which Canadian nationalism evolved' (p. xi).

edges.relationship: The English-Canadian national tradition analysed as historiography: its major figures, their nationalism and its limits (1976; 2nd ed. 1986)
edges.evidence_note: His own statement (1976 preface, reprinted 1986; Google Books snippet view of the 1986 second edition (volume jRN6AAAAMAAJ, University of Michigan copy; preface page not reported by Google), with the 1976 edition (bix6AAAAMAAJ) checked for the preface opening and contents. Snippets are short fragments; the continuous text was not read): 'This study is an examination of aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century. It deals with the central teachings of the major figures - George Wrong, Adam Shortt, Chester Martin, Harold Innis, Arthur Lower, Frank Underhill, Donald Creighton and William Morton - and also, in a less detailed fashion, with a more numerous group of other professional scholars who shaped the way Canadians understood their past'; 'The main emphasis is on the creative edge of historical writing and on those authors who broke the traditional patterns of interpretation'; 'Written history represents a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'. The 1976 conclusion, as Allen Mills quotes it (CJPST 1977, pp. 134–137, read in full): 'Canada's historians have all been nationalists of various hues, and sometimes their judgments about what was central to the past and what was peripheral arose as much from divergent conceptions of nationality as from disagreements about interpretations of the same evidence' (p. 259; Mills p. 136). The 1986 edition replaces that conclusion with a chapter on 'the vast exfoliation of historical literature over the last twenty years' (preface to the second edition). There 'A few historians in the sixties, moreover, subjected the tradition in which they had grown up to searching criticism. J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261), and he quotes Careless (1969) that the 'nation-building approach' 'neglects and obscures even while it explains and illuminates' (p. 262); social history's 'initial impact was to magnify the diversity of Canadian history' (p. 298). In-period reception. Mills: the book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada' and 'is really about' its eight 'superluminaries' (p. 135); 'his description of all Canadian historians as nationalists places much too much weight on that over-used term', since they 'have very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); but 'Berger's claim that Canadian historians have been generally unconcerned to explore the group loyalties of class, region, culture and family is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137). Terry Cook (Archivaria 5, 1977–78, pp. 198–203, read in full) calls it 'a remarkably subtle analysis of major trends in Canadian historiography' that 'transcends historiography to become an intellectual history of English Canada in the twentieth century' (p. 202). (Cook gives the 'nation-building' passage at p. 263 of the 1976 edition without naming Careless; the 1986 text attributes it to Careless.) Karr (1989, p. 161): 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote.' The French-Canadian limit is his own choice, explained in the preface: 'two language traditions have, in historical thought as well as in other non-political spheres, occasionally touched and intersected, but in general they have been preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”', and a comparison 'must rest on preliminary appraisals of the individual traditions'; 'the two traditions of historical writing flowed in separate channels' (p. 181). Ronald Rudin (1997; snippet view) shares 'Berger's belief that historical writing can “reveal a good deal about the intellectual climate in which it was composed”' but does 'not accept his assumption, implicit in Writing of Canadian History, that historians across the twentieth century have been united by their search for the truth' (p. 4), and finds that 'Berger failed, however, to consider the way in which Groulx had, by the 1930s, altered his view of the Dollard affair' (p. 58). Gregory Kealey (1982, reprinted 1995; snippet view) notes that the Marxist Stanley Ryerson 'was not considered for systematic evaluation in The Writing of Canadian History' (1995, p. 84), while finding 'little to argue with' in Berger's 1986 summary of the labour-history debate (1995, p. 18).

edges.relationship: The liberal nationalist account of imperialism as a colonial past defeated by Canadian nationalism, criticised (1970)
edges.evidence_note: His own words (1970; Google Books snippet view of the 2013 second edition (volume -Y-BAAAAQBAJ); its pages 3–265 reprint the 1970 text with the same pagination (Monet 1972 cites pp. 132 and 261 for passages found on those pages here). Snippets are short fragments returned by search; the continuous text was not read). The interpretation he set out to revise: 'The conflict between imperialism and nationalism added up to a struggle between the past and the future, the desire to remain a colony and the wish to be a free nation. Once this framework was accepted, it was easy to account for the failure of imperialism: it succumbed to Canadian nationalism. The main outlines of this interpretation survived largely because of the great influence of O. D. Skelton's biography of Laurier and because of the long dominance of a particular school of Canadian historiography of which it was the finest expression. This so-called liberal nationalist school has lately come under some penetrating scrutiny, its insufficiencies have been exposed and its continued relevance questioned. Naturally, its interpretation of imperialism has also been found wanting, at least by implication' (p. 9). Against it he argued that critics who attacked imperialism for 'its hostility to “Canadian nationalism”' 'really meant that they believed it incompatible with that kind of nationalism which they endorsed' (p. 9). In-period corroboration that this was the received English-Canadian view: Jacques Monet (RHAF 1972, read in full) writes that the imperialists 'ont eu très mauvaise presse parmi les historiens du Canada' and that English-Canadian historians, 'partisans pour la plupart de l'explication de l'équipe gagnante', saw them as 'des conservateurs retardataires' (p. 274); Berger 'vient maintenant nuancer ces jugements... téméraires' (p. 274). The same judgement runs into his historiography: in The Writing of Canadian History (1976) the main criticism of English-Canadian historians, as Allen Mills reads it (1977, read), is that they wrote 'as if they were contributing to pressing matters of contemporary public concern, especially the matter of national survival' (Mills's words, pp. 135–136). A counter-critique: Graham Carr (JCS 1982; journal abstract only) argues that 'revisionists such as Carl Berger, while ostensibly challenging Whig assumptions about imperialism/nationalism, actually share many of the traditional views'. The arrow records Berger's criticism of a position, the liberal nationalist account of imperialism; it does not claim that the national-tradition historians shared one view, and Skelton, whom he names, has no atlas entry.

edges.relationship: 'Limited identities': the regional, ethnic and class identities Canadians have, proposed as the place where 'Canadianism' might be found (1967), a phrase Careless made a programme (1969)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 'Canadian Centennial Cerebrations', International Journal 22:4 (1967), pp. 659–663: the opening, read in the OpenAlex text of the article, attacks Canadian Dimension's 'Open Letter to Canadian Nationalists', likens it to Canada First's 1874 manifesto and asks 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (p. 659). The limited-identities sentence was not read on Cook's page; Buckner quotes it (2000, p. 4): 'Perhaps instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found'. Taken up: Careless (CHR 1969; unread here, quoted by Buckner, p. 4) held that the 'Canadian experience' must be 'discerned and defined' through the 'limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook'. Buckner (p. 5) writes that 'Cook and Careless' embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, quoting Cook's 1970 essay as reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (p. 213): 'Nationalism by nature tends strongly to centralism and uniformity: Canada is by nature federal, sectional and pluralist'; 'historians in Atlantic Canada eagerly espoused the concept of “limited identities”, but their motivations were rather different' (p. 5). In period, Buckner's 1988 abstract (recorded in cdng_buckner_1988, not re-read) calls it 'the catch phrase of the Canadian historical profession in the 1960s' and judges it 'premature to abandon'. Criticism: Reid (1987, opening, recorded in cdng_reid_1987) notes that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result'; Gauvreau (1991, p. 164 n. 10) writes that limited identities 'has underwritten much of the “new social history”', which, like the older national history, 'marginalizes religious history'; Buckner (2000, p. 12) writes 'I think it implied to Cook and Careless' that national identity was the sum of component identities, calls that idea 'nonsensical', and argues that 'All identities are socially constructed'. Influence rather than contribution: Cook named the identities but wrote no regional history, and later questioned region as a unit of analysis (edge 2). The roster row calls him a precursor.

edges.relationship: Region questioned as a unit of analysis: regional history's strengths and weaknesses weighed (1977), and regions recast as provinces, 'a concept whose time has gone' (1983)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own review essays in Acadiensis, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (7:1, Autumn 1977, pp. 110–115), reviewing Bercuson's Canada and the Burden of Unity among other books, notes 'the tendency to see regionalism as a virtue of Canadian life rather than an obstacle to Canadian unity' (p. 110). Bercuson's contributors assume 'that Canadian history is best understood from a regional perspective' (p. 112), but 'neither he nor anyone else in the book attempts to define the term' (p. 114); 'the “regional” approach to Canadian history, and to its discontents, has both strengths and weaknesses. The whole may not be greater than the parts, but it is at least the sum of them' (p. 115). 'Regionalism Unmasked' (13:1, Autumn 1983, pp. 137–142), reviewing L. D. McCann's Heartland and Hinterland (1982): 'I have begun to doubt seriously the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions, though regionalism as a rationalization of certain interests may have some reality' (p. 140); McCann's definition of region 'applies at least as well, and perhaps better, to a province as to a region. So why not call a region what it really is — a province' (p. 140); with Cole Harris's chapter, the book 'can really lead to no other conclusion than that, as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (p. 141). He qualifies this: 'Stripped of its rhetoric there remains with the regional approach, especially as practised by historical geographers, a legitimate preoccupation with some profoundly important aspects of our history: class, sex, family, ethnicity, for example' (p. 141), and he calls Wynn's Maritimes chapter 'the finest section of the book' (p. 138). In-period response: Buckner (2000, pp. 8–10) cites both reviews, though he dates the first 1974 and renders 'whose time is gone' where the 1983 page reads 'has gone'. He calls the fragmentation charge 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8) and holds that the Atlantic Provinces 'had legitimate grievances within Confederation' (p. 10), adding that he was 'initially ... as skeptical as Cook' (p. 10). The critique targets the regional framework and heartland–hinterland synthesis, not regional research as such.

edges.relationship: The Laurentian view criticised as regional rather than national, and the national school read as superseded (1977–83)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (Acadiensis 7:1, 1977, p. 110): 'The so-called national schools have, in reality, had a rather obviously regional focus. Those who live in the Valley of the Fraser, the Red or the Restigouche can hardly accept the Laurentian view of Canadian history as “national”, unless, of course, they are content to be considered as “colonials” — a point made long ago by W. L. Morton. And the other nationalist themes fare little better.' 'Regionalism Unmasked' (Acadiensis 13:1, 1983, p. 137): 'the so-called “national” approach to the interpretation of the Canadian past has come under a destructive barrage of criticism' (the decade before it is garbled in the text layer); Berger's The Writing of Canadian History (1976) 'might be viewed as a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' (1946) 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis: the metropolitan-hinterland relationship was not one of equality'. In-period context: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) sets limited identities (edge 1) against a post-war consensus of 'liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill' and 'conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey' for whom the nation-state was the frame of reference. Limits: Cook credits the point to Morton; he co-wrote a Centenary Series volume (1974); and by Buckner's account (p. 8) he 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”' in 1977 ('The Golden Age of Canadian Historical Writing', Historical Reflections; unread here). The critique is of the Laurentian claim to speak for the nation, not of the staple studies' economics. edge_805 (cdn_regional → cdn_national_tradition, critique) carries the regional historians' version of the argument.

edges.relationship: The Regenerators: late Victorian social criticism read as the replacement of individual by social salvation, and the sacred becoming secular (1985)
edges.evidence_note: The book is unread here: UTP and De Gruyter refused automated access, and the Internet Archive copy is borrow-only. Its contents are recorded in crr_cook_1985, including the closing chapter 'The Sacred Becomes the Secular'. Cook's words are known as quoted in in-period readings. Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 161–162) quotes 'the orthodox Christian preoccupation with man's salvation was gradually replaced by a concern for social salvation' and 'the substitution of theology, the science of religion, with sociology, the science of society' (Regenerators, p. 4); Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (p. 6); social conservatism 'went hand in hand with scientific conservatism, and both were founded on religious conservatism' (p. 12); and social regeneration became 'a substitute for the formidable labour of reformulating theological doctrine' (p. 229). Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes that the book's subjects 'almost never alluded to the cultivation of a national sentiment' (p. 6). Gaffield's review (History: Reviews of New Books 14:5, 1986, p. 144; scanned page read by OCR and checked against the image) summarizes it: 'the call for social salvation emerged from a strong religious commitment but led to increasing secularization', and Cook 'treats religious thinking as an independent factor'. Contested in period. Gauvreau (1991) calls it 'important' but says it 'does not fully resist the temptation to view the 19th-century religious experience in relation to the 20th-century mind-set' (p. 161). He reads it as a '“neo-conservative” appropriation' of Allen's categories (p. 163); 'The appearance of The Regenerators in 1985 marked the beginning of the assault on Allen's position' (p. 163 n. 9). He adds that 'the emerging consensus seems to be away from “military metaphors” of the type employed by Cook' (p. 164). Van Die, he reports, 'ultimately accepts Cook's central thesis of the decline and irrelevance of Protestant religion, but does not agree with the conflict model' (p. 173). Marshall (CCHA Historical Studies 1993–94, web text without page numbers) names 'the secularization thesis outlined by McKillop, Cook, and Marshall' as Gauvreau's target and cites Regenerators pp. 228–32 (n. 6). Laverdure's 1998 review (crr_laverdure_1998, not re-read) says Christie and Gauvreau 'challenge the secularization thesis, most strongly advocated by Ramsay Cook … and David Marshall'. Karr (1989, p. 163 n. 21) finds 'an equally forceful Ontario bias' answering Allen's Western one. The name 'secularization thesis' is the critics', as the strand note says.

edges.relationship: An ecological interpretation of early Canadian history: contact as the interaction of ecologies, 'cabbages, at least as much as kings' (1990)
edges.evidence_note: Reuses the reading recorded on 2026-10-13 for the environment-family drafts (pe131_extras_cook_1990; canon-evidence-canada.md, text C1). It was not re-read for this entry because Project MUSE refused automated access. Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (Trent, October 1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) starts from Morton's 1946 remark that history 'is concerned with ecology too' (p. 5): 'It is an insight which I would like to try to build upon' (p. 6). He marks a break with the staple historians: 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), while 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus. They are no longer much concerned with explaining the impact of the environment on man; it is the impact of man on nature that is at the centre of their work' (p. 7). Following Crosby, 'contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13). His conclusion: 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world' (p. 15, as recorded in canon-evidence-canada.md; not in the source's verification note). In-period reading: Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 164–165 n. 12), arguing about Cook's religious history, called the lecture his 'recent “conversion experience” concerning the happy convergence of nature and culture'. Later reading, labelled: Wynn (2004, p. 33, recorded in pe131_extras_wynn_2004) quotes Cook's claim that Canadian historical writing 'has always been concerned with the environment' to describe Canadians who 'seemed to wonder what all the fuss was about'. A contribution, not a founding. edge_913 (harold_a_innis → environment) carries his continuity claim and Forkey's 1998 rejection of it; this edge carries his own ecological reading of contact.

edges.relationship: Between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians': class, ethnicity and gender as what Canadians share, and identities as contingent and multiple (1993–2000)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own words. 'The New History of Atlantic Canada' (Acadiensis 23:1, Autumn 1993, pp. 146–152, read in full) came between Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991–92) and Granatstein's book (1998): 'one of the sweet ironies in the arid debate between “nationalists” and “limited identitarians” on historiography is that neither side appears to recognize that class, ethnicity and gender describe what groups of Canadians have in common, while “nationalism” most often provokes divisions — “regionalism”!' (p. 146). He holds that 'for all the emphasis on differences during recent decades, Canadians from all regions and linguistic groups have, in fact, been growing more alike, at least in aspiration if not in reality' (p. 146). His 2000 CHR forum essay (pp. 260–265 per Buckner's n. 15) is read only in its abstract: the 'limited identities' hypothesis 'has played a major role in the flowering of social history whose dominance is now being called into question by proponents of a renewed “national” approach'; the debate ignores 'the easy assumption that identities, limited or national, are essential rather than contingent', and 'it is too often forgotten that identities are multiple rather than single'. Context: Bliss's abstract (1991–92) asks historians to remember 'that their subject, after all, is Canada' and does not name Cook. Buckner (2000) writes that Cook in 1995 called the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8; Canada, Quebec and the Uses of Nationalism, 2nd ed., p. 230, unread here). Buckner then groups Bliss, Granatstein and Owram with Careless's later view that the search for limited identities had 'gone too far' (p. 9). A contribution: Cook is a root of the debate (edge 1) and a respondent who in 1993 placed himself outside both camps.

edges.relationship: Nationalism as an object of criticism: English-Canadian nationalist intellectuals read from Canada First to the 1960s, against a 'strait-jacket identity' (1967–71)
edges.evidence_note: Cook's own text, 1967 (opening read in the OpenAlex text): Canadian Dimension's call for a union of nationalists 'of all parties' is set beside the 1874 call of 'William Foster and his exuberant young friends' (Canada First), and he answers 'Who says Canadian nationalism is difficult to define? Jobs!' (International Journal 22:4, p. 659). Two passages from 1970 are known only through quotation. Karr (Acadiensis 1989, p. 162) quotes Cook (Saturday Night, April 1970): 'Every generation of Canadian nationalist intellectuals ... seems to play the part of Sisyphus. Their permanent task is to push the millstone of Canadian nationalism up a steep mountain, only to find that it rolls back down again to await the labour of the next generation. This means that much of Canadian intellectual history sounds like a broken record'. Buckner (2000, p. 4) quotes the 1970 South Atlantic Quarterly essay, reprinted in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 197–214): Canada 'stubbornly refuses to exchange its occasionally anarchic pluralism for a strait-jacket identity. Perhaps it is this heterogeneous pluralism itself that is the Canadian identity'. In-period reading: Karr (1989, p. 162) writes that 'it was Ramsay Cook who did so much to heighten English Canada's understanding of French-Canadian nationalism who led the anti-national crusade', and that 'While it may be easy for many to agree with Cook's belittling of this recurring obsession with national identity, there are problems inherent in extremes on both sides'. His n. 18 adds: 'while Cook is opposed to divisive nationalism, he is a centralist and appears to be searching for a cohesive, positive form of national consensus' (p. 162). Gaffield (1986, p. 143) calls him 'one of Canada's major anglophone “windows” on francophone Québec'. The Maple Leaf Forever and Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966) are unread here. The Regenerators' place in this field is carried by edge_825.

edges.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. Clark's at the 1974 CHA meeting that 'it serves no useful purpose to work with such categories or concepts as metropolis and hinterland when what is metropolis can also be considered hinterland' (p. 107); both are quoted-in witnesses, not read here. Davis's own judgment: Careless, combining Gras's ecological model with the Laurentian school's elites, 'has produced a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research' (p. 102); his interpretation 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'the Gras-Careless statement of metropolitanism is weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103). Davis also reports that Careless disclaimed 'such a metropolitan “thesis”' in 1973 while keeping the 'approach' (p. 96, quoting Acadiensis 3, 1973). edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition) stays: it records the urban historians' critique at group level.

edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, and the frontierism Canadian historians took from it, criticised as environmental determinism; the frontier recast as a dependent of the metropolis (1954)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954), read in full. He summarises Turner's thesis that 'the greatest formative influence' in American history had been 'the open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6) and judges: 'This was environmental determinism at its most forthright. The wilderness and the men it produced had made America' (p. 7). Against it he sets the metropolitan reading: the frontier's culture 'originally stems from a metropolitan community; at root, learning and ideas radiate from there—and thus is Turner answered' (p. 18); 'the frontier, far from being essentially independent and self-reliant, is in the largest sense a dependent' (p. 18); and 'the functioning of metropolitanism may do more to explain the course of Canadian history than concepts of frontierism borrowed from the United States and set forth before the significance of the modern metropolis was clear' (p. 20). 'At any rate, frontierism, along with earlier schools and approaches, has had its use and its day' (p. 21). His qualifications are kept: 'Defenders of Turner might claim that he had not proposed a frontier hypothesis as the only key to American history' (p. 7); the frontier thesis 'proper' was never 'adopted as fully or dogmatically in Canada as it was in the United States—and there, of course, it has long been the subject of qualification and criticism' (p. 1); Canadian environmentalists took over 'the general approach and mood of Turner and company ... rather than the precise frontier thesis, which received little direct application in Canada' (p. 6). He draws on American critics of Turner (Hayes, Fox, Schlesinger Jr.; pp. 7–8) and on Canadian ones (McDougall 1929, Stanley 1940; p. 10, n. 21). The critique is therefore aimed at Turner's thesis and above all at its Canadian adaptation; the Canadian historians he names sit in cdn_national_tradition and are covered by edge 1. In-period reading: Davis (1985, p. 95, read) calls the article 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'. Davis (p. 109) also quotes Careless on television saying of Turner's thesis that 'like any view of history which gets oversimplified, overpopularized, it becomes untrue; it becomes a myth' (undated, a quoted-in witness). No reply by a Turnerian historian was found or read.

edges.relationship: Cook's phrase 'limited identities' made a programme for Canadian history (1969), and region read through the metropolitan systems that structure it (1979–89)
edges.evidence_note: The 1969 article (CHR 50:1, pp. 1–10) is unread here; its wording comes from two witnesses. Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, p. 4, read): Careless 'insisted that the “Canadian experience” must be “discerned and defined” through the “limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook”', and concluded that 'the whole may indeed be greater than the sum of its parts, producing through its internal relationships some sort of common Canadianism'. Careless himself, in 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; a lecture given in 1979; read in full, web text without page numbers), summarises the article as noting that these identities 'had tended to bulk larger for Canadians in their history than any identification with overall national patterns of values and attitudes', and quotes its p. 10: 'by pursuing a line largely of sociocultural inquiry, one may hope to uncover satisfactions in the limited identities ... which have added up to some positive balance of satisfaction with Canada itself'. The phrase is Cook's: Careless wrote that he 'did not invent the term “limited identity”, but acquired it from an article by Ramsay Cook, cited in my own article — which was thus essentially a commentary on his initial idea' (1981, n. 1); Buckner (p. 4) says Cook 'coined' it and Careless 'popularized' it. This edge carries Careless's programme, not the coinage. The 1981 lecture joins it to metropolitanism: regionalist historians often present 'an over-simple dichotomy' between a metropolitan central Canada and their own region, whereas 'regions are structured into metropolitan systems both within and beyond their territories'; 'Metropolitanism is not the antithesis of regionalism. Each is inherent in the other'. Frontier and Metropolis (1989) is unread; Rick Szostak's review (Journal of Economic History 50:2, 1990, pp. 499–501, read) reports that in it 'Cities become the foci of regional identity' and that Atlantic Canada 'develops a regional identity despite having no one dominant metropolis' (p. 500). In-period reception: the 1973 bibliography by Hann, Kealey, Kealey and Warrian opened with 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for ... a historical appreciation of the varieties of “limited identities” that constitute Canada' (as Careless quotes it in 1981; a quoted-in witness). Criticism: Buckner (2000, p. 10) answers critics who treat regional studies as, 'as Careless and Granatstein seem to believe, a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state'; Robert Irwin (Journal of Canadian Studies 32:3, 1997; abstract only) argues that prairie identity 'must be understood as an autonomous layer of consciousness rather than a “limited identity” within a national consciousness'; Szostak found the book 'descriptive rather than analytical' and expected readers to be 'left unconvinced' (p. 500). Buckner (p. 5) also notes the different motives: Cook and Careless embraced the concept partly in response to Quebec separatism, Atlantic historians for other reasons. edge_805 and edge_814 stay as group-level arrows.

edges.relationship: The metropolis–hinterland approach, taken up by Canadian urban historians in the 1970s and then contested by them (1954–85)
edges.evidence_note: His own statements. The 1954 article proposes the metropolis and its hinterland as a field of study, including 'social and cultural associations' as well as economic ties (pp. 17–18), and names Masters's The Rise of Toronto as the closest application (p. 17). In 1981 he writes that 'urban history' grew within regional writing because cities 'are also centres that focus and structure regions or sub-regions about them. The interplay of city and region thus demands and has received attention', and that he had 'always sought to emphasize the reciprocal and complementary nature of the relations between the great city and the territory it dominates' (Manitoba History no. 1, web text). Davis (1985) lists his urban-history articles: 'Urban Development in Canada', Urban History Review 1 (1974), and 'Metropolis and Region', Urban History Review 3 (1979) (nn. 6, 11; unread). In-period reception, from Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), read in full: 'In the 1970s metropolitanism helped preside over the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history', and according to Artibise and Linteau (1984) the articles by Careless on metropolis and region 'marked, in some ways at least, the self-conscious beginning of urban history' in Canada (p. 96; a quoted-in witness); urban historians 'have remained the most faithful to the metropolitan concept of J.M.S. Careless, the godfather of their subdiscipline' (p. 96); Gilbert Stelter called the metropolitan thesis in 1977 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history' (p. 96, quoted). A contribution, contested within the field: Davis argues that 'there is no single metropolitan thesis' (p. 107), that Careless's approach 'has fallen into desuetude in historical circles' (p. 103), that Artibise found the metropolis/hinterland concept 'not really a theory that explain[ed] Canadian urban development' (p. 103, quoted), and that urban historians 'might do better by abandoning the metropolitan approach altogether' (abstract, p. 95). Davis also records Careless's own reserve: he would 'disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96, quoting 1973). This is a Canadian contribution; it does not claim that Dyos's or US urban history drew on Careless. edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition, critique) stays: it records the field's rejection of metropolitanism, this edge the field's use of it.

edges.relationship: Limited identities and his own early warning against particularism (1969, 1979–81) as the ground of the later fragmentation debate
edges.evidence_note: His own words, 'Limited Identities — Ten Years Later' (lecture of 1979, Manitoba History no. 1, 1981; read in full, web text). Ten years after 1969 he sees 'a massive outpouring' of writing on regional interests, cultural discords and class disparities in which 'national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted', and says: 'I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood, when he declared “Lord, I know I prayed for rain — but this is ridiculous.”' He disclaims responsibility for the flood ('I scarcely caused the flood') and does not withdraw the concept: 'I do feel the concept has had much value, and still has'. But 'Unity in diversity' now seems rather 'diversity Unlimited', and 'limited identities remain crucial subjects for the historian's regard — but they should not limit his own perception'; 'Now the task is to cut the sight-lines through'. In-period readings: John G. Reid (Acadiensis 16:2, 1987) records that during the 1980s 'concern has increasingly been expressed that fragmentation has been the result', an argument made in Canada by Careless (graph verification note; not re-read here). Buckner (Acadiensis 30:1, 2000, read): Careless 'too had come to the conclusion that the search for limited identities had gone too far and threatened the very existence of the Canadian nation-state' (pp. 8–9, citing this lecture); 'More recently the same point has been made, somewhat crudely, by Michael Bliss and Jack Granatstein and with greater sophistication by Doug Owram' (p. 9). Buckner contests the premise, calling the 'so-called fragmentation of the historical profession' 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8). An influence as precursor, not participation: his texts predate the 1991–99 exchanges, and no debate text read here names him except Buckner's. Bliss's 1991–92 article (abstract only) does not name him; Bliss is not presented as answering him. edge_814 (cdn_regional → who_killed_debate) stays: it records regional history as the debate's ground.

edges.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

edges.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
edges.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.
