edges.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
edges.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.

edges.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

edges.relationship: Gender in the making of class: a women's town and a men's town, Paris and Hanover, Ontario (1985–90)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985): 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations', with women's historians and historians of childhood, 'have reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42); 'Skill, too, is a socially constructed category' (pp. 42–43). Of the Marxist analysis in Women at Work, Ontario, 1850–1930 (1975) she writes, quoting feminist critics (n. 20: Phillips and Taylor; Hartmann), that it 'explains why a hierarchy of labour is necessary within the waged labour force, but tells us nothing about why women end up at the bottom of this hierarchy' (p. 43). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990; unread here) compares Paris and Hanover, Ontario. Heron, a labour historian, reviewing it (CHR, 1991, read in full): 'the most exhilarating, challenging book to appear in modern Canadian social history in many years'; it 'integrates and surpasses' women's, labour, technological and economic history, and 'Parr gives the boot to neo-classical analysis, simplistic Marxism, and radical feminism' (p. 218). He quotes its introduction that 'the parts and proportions of the social landscape covered by class and gender alter' (p. 10) but finds that in the 1949 Paris strike 'she has suppressed the impact of class where it was undeniably a crucial force' (p. 220). From her own figures he suggests that 'the portrait of the "women's town" may be slightly misleading' (p. 219). He also finds that she downplays the wars and the state and 'seldom makes any reference to the considerable Canadian literature on work, class, gender, or small-town life' (pp. 220–21). He concludes that she 'has pushed us onto new terrain where gender is neither ignored nor is it given a monocausal explanatory force' (p. 221). Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991) sees 'a more dynamic alternative to the old and stale studies that focused more on workers' industrial and organizational activities', while doubting conclusions drawn from 'the testimony of seven women' (p. 175). Dennis (EcHR, 1991) calls it 'an important contribution to the literature of labour history and locality studies' (p. 762). A contribution from inside the field's gender strand, alongside Sangster (1989) and Bradbury (1993). It does not claim that labour history lacked gender before 1990. edge_842 and edge_889 (cdn_women_gender → cdn_working_class) already carry the entry-level contribution and critique.

edges.relationship: British child immigrants as labouring children (1977–80), and childhood as a history of power (1985)
edges.evidence_note: In-period. Her Yale PhD (1977), 'The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924', is recorded in the AHA Directory of History Dissertations (record 45612; adviser Robin Winks). Drystek's review of Labouring Children (Archivaria 11, 1980–81, read in full) names the thesis as the source of its sample of 997 Barnardo case histories (p. 241). He quotes the book's aims: a 'study of the life and work of child immigrants in Britain and Canada' (p. 13) that would 'reveal a darker side of evangelicalism, of turn-of-the-century childhood, and of Canadian rural life than the record has so far been allowed to express' (p. 12). His reading is critical: 'because of the authors' almost uniformly negative approach, the study is of limited value', the sample's statistical basis is unexplained, and 'the argument that a British child immigrant suffered a special burden is not convincing' (pp. 241–42). The book itself is unread here. Her own words (Atlantis, 1985) turn the subject into a question about power: she finds it troubling to treat women and children 'as part of one subject', admits to being 'part of a group who wrote, reviewed, lectured and squabbled this cluster into convention', and asks 'Is it nature which ties women and children together as subjects? Clearly not' (p. 39); the family 'is experienced by members of different generations in very different ways' (p. 44). She also edited Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982; title-level, see edge_792). A contribution among the field's early works, not its origin: Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) precedes it.

edges.relationship: Disaggregating the sexual division of labour: gender and class compared across workplaces, read beyond Canada (1988–93)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the CSSH article of 1988 (first-page extract read, p. 511) observes that 'economists and feminist theorists have been interested in sexual divisions as general features of the economic or sex/gender system rather than as boundaries between tasks forged in defined contexts by particular clashes of interest', and that 'most analysts have dealt with gender division as a characteristic of the work force as a whole'. Reviews of The Gender of Breadwinners outside Canada (all read in full): Benson (JAH, 1993, p. 1630) writes that 'few historians have successfully integrated the discussion of these two fundamental relationships' and that 'Parr joins this small but growing group'. On p. 1631 Benson continues: 'Like others influenced by post-structuralist theory, she emphasizes the shifting and multivalent meanings often obscured by dualisms'; Parr 'gives gender and class coordinate roles in her analysis but downplays ethnicity'. Dennis (EcHR, 1991) finds that she 'goes far beyond previous accounts of connections between capitalism and patriarchy' (p. 761) but faults graphs that 'cavalierly use straight lines to connect a handful of isolated observations' (p. 762). Bertaux (JEH, 1992) wants 'a basic quantitative summary of work force data' (p. 240) but concludes that 'the topic of gender and work is not strictly a "women's issue"' (p. 241). The book itself is unread here. This records reception in international journals, not adoption. Optional: edge_840 (cdn_women_gender → gender) already links the Canadian field to the international entry.

edges.relationship: Postwar Canadian consumption as a politics of nation, class and gender: domestic goods, designers and householders (1999)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the abstract of 'Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada' (ILWCH 55, 1999, a special issue on class and consumption) reads 'How much consumption matters is a cultural difference, a shared national predicament, a politics grounded in the circumstances of class, and learned as a gendered responsibility', and asks 'When producers were not paramount in the regulation of consumption, to what priorities was commerce subsidiary?' Domestic Goods (1999) is unread here; as Brush quotes it (EH.NET, 2000, read in full), it is 'an archeology of the material, moral, and economic choices and constraints which formed Canadian commodity culture in the two decades after the Second World War' (p. 17). It asks 'How much can citizens talk back to manufacturers and the state about domestic goods?' (pp. 3–4). It sets itself against accounts that 'naturalize[d] these hortatory American norms as the intrinsic qualities of "consumer society"' (p. 11), and it places studies of material culture 'into unaccustomed company' (p. 3). Brush notes that Parr 'locates the history of consumption as a history primarily of women as consumers, in contrast to the male-dominated fields of design and manufacturing'. Criticism: Owram (BC Studies 129, 2001, read in full) finds the book's 'strength is in its parts rather than in some seamless thesis' (p. 103). He reads her as arguing that 'the assumption of consumer sovereignty is facile' (p. 104), and answers that 'Canadians, both men and women, preferred Fords to Volvos, and that is what they got' (p. 105). edge_843 (cdn_women_gender ↔ consumption, comparison) is title-level; this edge adds read evidence.

edges.relationship: Embodied, sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change in Canada, 1953–2003 (2006–10)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2006–2011; no claim here concerns her work before 2000. Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (UBC Press, 2010) is unread here. As Jackson quotes it (Senses and Society 6:2, 2011, read in full), Parr seeks to move beyond 'representations . . . in language . . . , to open interpretive space in which to study the robust materiality of technologies, environments, and the everyday, to encounter them as directly and as fleshly as possible' (p. 9). Jackson describes chapters on the NATO base at Gagetown, nuclear power and heavy water on Lake Huron, the St Lawrence Seaway at Iroquois, the Columbia River reservoir and Walkerton's water, each read through a sense ('Smell and Risk', 'Taste and Expertise'). She adds that Parr counts proprioception, kinesthetics and proxemics among the senses (pp. 225–27). Jackson places the book in the UBC Press Nature/History/Culture series (p. 225). Rumiel (Left History 15:1, 2011, read in full) notes 'the people whose lives and senses of self had been transformed' by megaprojects (p. 189). She suggests that 'a comparative analysis of a related case in a Canadian Aboriginal or Inuit community' was a missed opportunity (p. 189). The environmental line begins earlier with 'Smells Like?: Sources of Uncertainty in the History of the Great Lakes Environment' (Environmental History 11:2, 2006; metadata only). A contribution: it records her later field, not influence on environmental history's formation.

edges.relationship: Moral regulation as the formation of ethical subjectivity, carried out by philanthropies, churches and professions as well as the state: social purity in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991–92; the 1988 article with Weir is listed but unread)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full: 'I have argued elsewhere that the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests', though 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); she credits Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch with pioneering 'the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities' (p. 217). The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) is known here through in-period reviewers' quotations and through Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 University of Toronto Press reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C; partial preview, page images not viewable here because the viewing limit was reached), which keep the 1991 pagination: reformers sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' (p. 17; quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 316); purity work 'was not simply a question of banning obscene books or suppressing prostitution but was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17; quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124); the reform movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class' (p. 15; Dehli, p. 318); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; snippet, the last clause also quoted by Dehli, p. 317); '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations' (p. 166, as quoted by Wright 1995, p. 124). Her notes, seen only as snippets, place the concept: in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured' (n. 34, p. 171); Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity' (p. 173). Note 33 (p. 171) cites the 1988 article with Lorna Weir, which is unread here. In-period reception by historians. Tina Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, pp. 277–279, read) calls the book 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279). Donald Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, pp. 122–126 read) calls it a 'much talked about treatise' by 'a sociologist' (p. 122) and its concept of 'slippages' among class, gender, sexuality and race her 'most original' contribution (p. 124). Carolyn Strange and Tina Loo's Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada (1997; Google Books snippets, pp. 5, 63) write that 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation' (p. 5) and cite 'Mariana Valverde and others' on prostitution as 'the social evil' (p. 63). Mary Louise Adams's 'In Sickness and in Health: State Formation, Moral Regulation, and Early VD Initiatives in Ontario' (1994) is cited at title level only. In-period criticism. Loo finds the second argument, on philanthropy and the state, 'more asserted than proved' (p. 279). Kari Dehli (Historical Studies in Education, 1992, pp. 315–319, read) would draw 'not quite so sharply drawn' conclusions about state and civil society and finds that she moves 'quickly from analysis of discursive strategies ... to drawing conclusions about people's motives and intentions' (pp. 318–319). Wright judges her claim that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' 'untenable' and finds 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" ... conspicuously silent', so that 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (pp. 125–126). Chris McCormick (Atlantis, 1992, pp. 123–125, read) asks how her interpretations are made and judges that a 'thorough' reading of context is 'optimistic' (p. 123), while agreeing that 'Regulation is a better word than control' (p. 124). Sociologists reformulated the concept: Alan Hunt's 1997 abstract (read) treats moral regulation not as 'a specific moral arena' but as 'a component of all fields of social relations', a wider definition than hers; in Governing Morals (1999; snippets) he writes 'I do not take issue with Valverde's invocation of ethical subjectivity, but I emphasise the mundane features of self-governing' (p. 155). Dean (1994) and Ruonavaara (1997) are cited through their abstracts as on the moral_regulation node. A contribution, not a founding: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits them. Diseases of the Will (1998), on alcohol and the governance of the will, is title-level here (snippets only) and does not support this edge.

edges.relationship: Protestant reformers read as moral regulators rather than as religious actors, and the church historians' objection that this excised the churches from progressive thought (1991–96)
edges.evidence_note: Her object overlaps the field's. The book studies Methodist and Presbyterian church organizations, the Salvation Army, the WCTU, the YWCA and the National Council of Women (Dehli 1992, p. 316, read), with familiar reformers such as Chown, Shearer and Woodsworth (Loo 1992, p. 277, read). Her reading is regulatory: purity work 'was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17, quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124), and the discourse of moral reform 'needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' ('Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', 1992, p. 216, read). In-period objections from historians of religion and reform. Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) finds that 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift', suggests Richard Allen's typology of radical, progressive and conservative reformers, and holds that 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'. Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), known here only through Google Books search-within snippets: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187), and her analysis 'wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture', against which they set 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' among Protestant clergy (p. 188; n. 95, p. 328, cites her pp. 15, 112, 123–8). Their p. 187 summary attributes to her a state-centred hegemony that her own p. 165 qualifies ('the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'); the disagreement is recorded, not adjudicated. A comparison, as her roster row and edge_861 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform) have it: the criticism runs from the church historians to her, and she did not answer it in a text read here. The dispute is person-level, which is why it is drawn from her entry; edge_861 stays the field-level comparison.

edges.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

edges.relationship: Scott's poststructuralist programme criticised by a sympathetic reader, who suggested that it may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can do for historians, for passing over discourse analysis's bias towards 'the sociology of domination', and (1995) for setting theory against working-class history
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period words (1990 essay read in full; 1995 essay, pp. 329–332 read). 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?', Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990), pp. 227–236, reviews Scott's Gender and the Politics of History with Denise Riley's 'Am I That Name?'. She grants that Scott's approach 'has much to commend it' but finds her four elements of gender 'somewhat arbitrary' and asks whether the definition 'finally succeeds in transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230). Scott's case studies show limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231): there is 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott, does not discredit or make redundant discourse analysis' (p. 232). Scott's 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems', with a 'grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232), and 'It may be that she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work' (p. 233). She ends that 'Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233). 'Deconstructive Marxism', Labour/Le Travail 36 (1995), pp. 329–340 (pp. 329–332 read), sharpens the judgment: Scott 'made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway', and 'the book undoubtedly made an important contribution to the feminist analysis of both politics and history: but it did so, or at least gave the appearance of doing so, at the expense of working-class history' (p. 332). She criticises the other side too: 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding' (p. 332), and her note names Bryan Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (p. 332, n. 5). edge_891 (joan_wallach_scott → cdn_women_gender) already cites the 1990 essay as evidence of Canadian engagement with Scott; this edge records her own criticism of Scott's position, which edge_891 does not carry. A critique within broad sympathy, not a rejection: the qualifications above are part of the claim.

edge_824.relationship: Historical writing treated as a domain of English-Canadian intellectual history and its national preoccupation examined (1971–86)
edge_824.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Trofimenkoff (1979, p. 9, read): 'some of the people have suggested that the leit motiv of both English and French Canadian historical writing, in itself a domain of intellectual history, has been the concern for survival, a nationalist concern'; her note 4 cites Ramsay Cook's essays 'La Survivance French Canadian Style' and 'La Survivance English Canadian Style' in The Maple Leaf Forever (1971, pp. 114–40, 141–65; not read here). Karr (1989, p. 161, read) places Berger's analysis of 'the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote' among the English-Canadian intellectual historians' studies of nationalism. Berger's 1986 chapter records that 'J.M.S. Careless joined Ramsay Cook in condemning the undue emphasis on national history and unity' (p. 261, snippet view). The arrow records intellectual historians making the national tradition's writing an object of study; Berger's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (the Canadian persons Tier 1 revision).

edge_798.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, p. 5) calls the pre-1960s Canadian approach "similar to that of the consensus school in the United States": minimizing internal divisions and stressing what united Canadians. Davis (1985, p. 102) likewise says Careless's metropolitan interpretation "fits the mould of 'consensus' history". Comparison with the consensus half of the atlas entry only. Careless's 1954 article, read for revision 1.136, criticises the Canadian historians who adapted Turner's frontier thesis; that critique is the separate edge from his person entry (j_m_s_careless → progressive), not this comparison.

edge_858.evidence_note: Ruonavaara's abstract describes Corrigan and Sayer's framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with basic Marxist theory; Dean's abstract argues that problems in Corrigan's account are better formulated through Foucault's problematic of governmentality. Drawn as a contribution, the atlas's usual kind for Foucault's outgoing edges. Valverde's own acknowledgement (checked 2026-10-14 for revision 1.136, in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination): 'Following but modifying Foucault's approach, I take the term "discourses" to refer not to language as separate from the real world but rather to organized sets of signifying practices' (preface, p. x) and 'as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; also quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 317). Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, p. 123, read) reads her as modifying 'Foucault's archaeology' with 'an important commitment to social agency'. Strange and Loo (1997, p. 5, snippet): 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation'. Not a claim about every Canadian study in the roster.

edge_861.evidence_note: Valverde studies the moral fervour of Protestant social reformers (publisher description); the religion-and-reform entry studies the same churches and social gospel as religious history (Christie and Gauvreau 1996, title-level). The two fields read the reformers differently. In period, Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) asked Valverde's book to 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance', and Christie and Gauvreau (1996, p. xiii, Google Books snippet) said she and Doug Owram used 'a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches'. Those objections concern one book and are recorded on the edge from the mariana_valverde entry (revision 1.136); this field-level edge stays a comparison. Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. Comparison only.

rationale: Person entries go to thinkers whose frameworks students meet across fields (user, 2026-10-13); a field-bound big idea counts, as Wolfe's did, and so does a historical big idea that has declined, as Innis's did. Each Tier 1 name carries a framework the Canadian historiography names: metropolitanism, limited identities, the Laurentian thesis, imperialism as nationalism and the historiography of the field itself, gender and class together, moral regulation. Evidence: each draft's NOTES.md records what was read in full, in part, through in-period readers or in search-within snippets, and what was not read; snippet and reviewer-mediated quotations are labelled. Dissertation evidence is metadata only and never in entry text: Canadian History PhDs citing them (2009–2026) number 193 (Berger), 179 (Cook), 188 (Parr), 186 (Valverde), 103 (Creighton) and 102 (Careless), with readership dispersion 0.78–0.85; this measures Canadian reading, not importance.
